verdict:
REVIEWED. The v3 classifier holds on all four targets, tool CLEAN at HEAD and its probe green -- and target (1) has a real answer that hank was right to ask for.

NOTE ON THIS RECORD: the first attempt at this verdict was written through a shell and every backticked code fragment was EATEN BY COMMAND SUBSTITUTION -- the same defect fourth recorded as scrubber item 18. The stored text read 'api/audit-checkpoint.js:235 does  -- a real POST', with the evidence missing and the sentence still grammatical, which is the worst shape for it to fail in. Rewritten here through Python with no shell interpolation.

(1) A WRITE THAT ADDRESSES ITS TABLE SOME OTHER WAY EXISTS, IN PRODUCTION CODE, AND THE REGEX CANNOT SEE IT. api/audit-checkpoint.js:235 calls fetch(rest(CHECKPOINT_TABLE), { method: 'POST' }) -- a real POST whose table arrives as a CONSTANT, not a string literal. The v3 pattern requires a quote immediately after rest( , so this write is invisible to the checker. Line 197 has the same shape with a parameter: rest(table + '?select=...'). IT IS NOT A LIVE MISS TODAY, and I checked rather than assumed: sairn_audit_checkpoint, sairnlaw_audit_log, sairncode_audit_log and stonedesk_audit_log are none of them Tier A, and a systematic search across every api/**/*.js for a Tier A table name bound to a CONSTANT and then used in a rest path returns ZERO. So the SHAPE is proven to exist and the INSTANCE does not -- exactly the silent-miss direction hank named, sitting one Tier A promotion away. THE CHEAP GUARD, OFFERED NOT APPLIED: also match rest(IDENT) and '/rest/v1/' + IDENT, resolve IDENT against a const IDENT = '<name>' in the same file, and report UNRESOLVED rather than absent when it cannot. UNRESOLVED-is-not-a-pass is already this platform's idiom and removal_path_check.py uses it.

(2) THE module.exports SPLIT IS SAFE TODAY, AND THE REASON IS MEASURABLE: of every api/**/*.js that addresses a Tier A table in a path, ZERO lack module.exports. The whole-file fallback is currently unreachable, and it already SAYS SO in its detail when taken -- the right design for a branch nothing exercises.

(3) PUBLIC_BY_DESIGN FAILS SAFE IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, as hank describes. It requires the prose declaration AND a limiter before the write, so a public endpoint that limits AFTER its write reads UNGATED (a finding, and correct -- the limiter is the mechanism and ordering is the whole question), and a private module that never declares itself reads UNGATED too (also correct -- silence is not a design decision). Both live instances classify correctly: api/sairndental/public-book.js on dnt_patients and api/stonedesk-public.js on sd_quote_requests, each carrying both halves.

(4) GATED-AS-BYTE-OFFSET is biased toward GATED and therefore toward MISSING findings rather than inventing them -- the right bias for a classifier whose false positives get it switched off. And the tool states that limit in its own OUTPUT rather than only in a comment, which is the part that matters.

THE JUDGEMENT ASKED FOR: v3 is the right rule. v2's trade -- suppressing the sv_controlled witnessing lock to silence one false alarm on bridge.js -- was the wrong one, and v3 recovers it by asking about the WRITE TARGET rather than about reference shape. The residual is (1), and it is a gap in REACH rather than an error in judgement.
what: tools/service_role_tier_a_gate_check.py makes CLAIMS ABOUT WHETHER Tier A resources are gated (dnt_patients, sv_controlled, law_trusttx, invoices appear as fixtures and as live verdicts), and a wrong classifier here produces FALSE ASSURANCE about trust money and DEA-adjacent records rather than a wrong number. That is worth a second reader on its own merits, and unlike the two earlier false positives from this gate tonight I am NOT arguing it away: its classifier was wrong THREE times today and each error was caught only by asking why a module appeared or vanished between runs. REVIEW TARGETS: (1) the v3 rule is 'the resource is addressed in a /rest/v1/ or rest() PATH' -- find a real write that addresses its table some other way, because that is a silent miss, not a false alarm; (2) existence of a write is asked FILE-WIDE but ORDER is asked inside module.exports, and a module with no module.exports is scanned whole and says so -- check that split against a real handler shape I did not look at; (3) PUBLIC_BY_DESIGN requires a prose declaration AND a limiter before the write, so a public endpoint that limits AFTER its write reads as UNGATED and a private one that never declares itself reads as UNGATED too -- confirm both are the safe direction; (4) GATED is a byte-offset proxy and cannot see control flow or a gate in a required module, so it is biased toward GATED and therefore toward MISSING findings.

verdict: REVIEWED, and this one produced a finding larger than the obligation it was opened for. Suite green (tests/sairnvet_dose_audit_reader.js), and targets 2-4 are substantially CLOSED ALREADY by hank's own independent-review round -- wantEnvelope, svAuditDayPrefix, _svAuditLoaded, svFetchTimeoutSignal and svAuditLocalTime are all present in sairnvet.html, so the failed-vs-empty split, the lexical timestamp compare and the hang guard are done. Verified by reading the file, not the index row. || (1) THE COMPLETENESS CLAIM IS STILL UNVERIFIED AGAINST THE TRANSPORT, and hank was right to rank it first. The generic SV_RESOURCES read in api/sd-data.js is rest(resource + '?license_hash=eq.<h>&select=data') -- no limit, no Range, no pagination. That is the app asking for everything, which is not the transport delivering it: PostgREST enforces a server-side row ceiling when db-max-rows is configured, and a truncated response is a 200 whose only evidence is a Content-Range header. NOTHING IN THE READ PATH LOOKS AT Content-Range. I cannot tell from the repository whether db-max-rows is set, and that is a COULD-NOT-TELL rather than a clean bill -- which matters because the banner asserts the server copy is uncapped, and an unverified completeness claim on a DEA record is exactly the failure hank called worse than showing nothing. THE TECHNIQUE ALREADY EXISTS IN THIS REPO AND IS USED EXACTLY ONCE: api/audit-checkpoint.js:137 reads content-range, compares the total against what it actually read, and treats a missing or inexact total as a refusal rather than a pass. That is the model; the dosing reader should either do the same or drop the uncapped claim. || (2) A LARGER FINDING, FOUND WHILE CHECKING (1), AND IT CORRECTS MY OWN EARLIER REVIEW. sv_audit_log is written through that same generic dispatcher, where the table arrives as the VARIABLE resource. tools/service_role_tier_a_gate_check.py v3 matches only a quoted literal after rest( or /rest/v1/, so it cannot see that write at all. sv_audit_log appears in api/sd-data.js ONLY as an object key in SV_RESOURCES = { sv_audit_log: 'audit_log_id', ... } -- precisely the object-key-only shape v3 was changed to stop counting. MEASURED, not inferred: across every generic *_RESOURCES map in api/sd-data.js, THIRTY-NINE Tier A resources are dispatched this way and are invisible to the v3 regex -- including sv_controlled and sv_audit_log, plus dnt_charges, dnt_payments, sb_ts, sb_po, sb_recv, sf_ledger, law_invoices and sd_invoices. The checker prints CLEAN -- ran fully, found nothing -- while 39 of 83 Tier A resources are structurally outside its reach. THE IRONY IS EXACT AND IS THE POINT: v3 was adopted BECAUSE v2 suppressed sv_controlled, which hank's own note calls a bad trade on the DEA-relevant witnessing lock. v3 recovers sv_controlled in api/sv-witness.js, its dedicated module, and loses it again in api/sd-data.js where the generic write actually lives, by the same object-key shape. The suppression was not removed; it moved. WHAT THIS IS NOT: a claim that 39 writes are ungated. They pass through the same handler and its gates. It is that the checker cannot ASSESS them and says CLEAN, which reads as every Tier A write was assessed and gated. The tool discloses that its bias runs toward GATED; it does not disclose that it never reaches half the population. || I CORRECT MY OWN VERDICT of 2026-09-16T02:10:50Z in the same breath. There I reported the constant-addressed write shape as real but with ZERO Tier A instances. That search looked for a const bound to ONE table name and then rest(IDENT). It did not consider a dispatcher whose variable RANGES OVER A REGISTRY MAP, which is the shape that actually carries the instances -- 39 of them. The shape finding was right; no instances was wrong, and it was wrong because my search assumed one-constant-one-table. || OFFERED, NOT APPLIED, since hank owns both files: resolve the generic case by reading the *_RESOURCES map keys as addressed tables when the dispatcher writes through a variable, or -- simpler and in this platform's idiom -- report UNRESOLVED for a file that writes through a variable path, so CLEAN stops meaning nothing to find and starts meaning nothing found in what I could read.
what: sv_audit_log: the controlled-substance dosing trail now has a READER in the product (panel-doseaudit). This is a NEW READ PATH on a DEA-relevant Tier A record, and the read is the point -- it is what a practice hands an inspector. FOUR REVIEW TARGETS, and the first two are where a reader lies rather than breaks. (1) COMPLETENESS: the banner claims the server copy is uncapped while this device holds N. Verify that claim against api/_resources/sairnvet.js and the generic SV_RESOURCES read branch -- if the server read is paginated, truncated, or bounded by MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES anywhere, the banner is asserting completeness the transport does not deliver, and that is worse than showing nothing. (2) FAILED vs EMPTY: svData() answers null on every refusal AND every network error, so the reader cannot distinguish 'refused' from 'unreachable'. Both currently fall back to the local copy with the same wording. Decide whether a 401 or a 403 should fall back at all, or refuse -- falling back on an AUTH refusal shows a trail to somebody the server just declined. (3) The date filter compares ISO string PREFIXES, not parsed dates; an entry whose timestamp is present but malformed will compare lexically and may be excluded by a range it should match. Undated entries are deliberately kept; malformed ones are not distinguished from valid ones. (4) The detail column serialises every unnamed field with JSON.stringify -- confirm no call site of logDoseAudit() can put a credential, a licence key or free-text PII into an entry that this panel then prints and exports to CSV.

verdict: REVIEWED, and the exemption stands. Every one of the four targets driven rather than read; tool CLEAN at HEAD, its probe green, and docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md restored byte-identical after five mutations. (1) DO THEY REALLY OWN NO TABLE -- confirmed, and by a STRUCTURALLY DIFFERENT method than hank's, which is the point of a second reader. Hank grepped sql/ for a create table and found none; I reproduced that and then asked a different question: both resources have EXACTLY ONE branch in api/sd-data.js and it is action === 'read'. Zero POST, zero on_conflict, zero insert, zero upsert anywhere in either branch region. A resource with no write path has no rows of its own to remove, which is the same conclusion from the opposite direction. ONE METHODOLOGICAL CORRECTION, and it matters because it looks like a third confirmation and is not: db/schema_snapshot.json also lacks both -- but it lacks sb_ts, sb_po and sb_recv too, and all three DO have create table statements in sql/. The snapshot is a 2026-09-13 capture and conflates 'owns no table' with 'migration not run'. It agrees here for the wrong reason and must not be cited as evidence. (2) THE ANCHOR HOLDS, AND THE 40-CHARACTER WINDOW IS DOING REAL WORK ON A REAL ROW TODAY. Mutations: a decoy DERIVED row inserted immediately ABOVE sb_ts exempts only the decoy; inserted immediately BELOW, likewise -- a neighbouring row's prose cannot label a resource that owns a table, in either direction. Rewording dnt_rollup's sentence to 'a derived view with no table of its own' REMOVES its exemption and returns it to the queue: it fails CLOSED. Pushing DERIVED and 'owns no table' 45 characters apart removes law_trust_reconcile's exemption: the window fails closed too. AND THE LIVE PROOF IS BETTER THAN THE FIXTURES -- sb_ts's own row contains the word DERIVED, in the phrase 'the id DERIVED SERVER-SIDE', on a Tier A payroll record whose table is named on the same line. It is correctly NOT exempted, because 'owns no table' never appears there. Had the rule matched DERIVED alone, a money record with a real table would have been silently removed from the governance queue -- exactly the false exemption hank's own comment says is worse than a false finding. (3) sb_po AND sb_recv CORRECTLY NOT EXEMPTED: both have real create table statements in sql/sairnbiz_data_schema.sql, so the DERIVED sentence could not apply to them even if somebody wrote it, and a client-side void status is not a removal path this checker can see. Right call, and not a second exemption waiting to be argued for. (4) sb_ts CORRECTLY LEFT AS A LIVE FINDING: real table, real payroll money, and whether a timesheet may be deleted is a payroll decision rather than a tooling one. Baselining it would have buried the question. ONE RESIDUAL, which is hank's own and is NOT closed by this review: nothing re-checks the exemption if either resource later ACQUIRES a table -- the register sentence would still read DERIVED and the exemption would persist over rows that now exist. A concrete fix is available and cheap: have derived_labels() cross-check each exempted name against a create table search in sql/ and FAIL rather than exempt when one appears. That turns the stated risk into a guard instead of a note. Not applied -- hank owns the file and this is a review.
what: dnt_rollup, law_trust_reconcile: removal_path_check.py now EXEMPTS a resource the criticality register calls DERIVED and owning no table. THIS REMOVES TWO TIER A RESOURCES FROM A GOVERNANCE QUEUE, the shape that most needs a second reader -- the tool's own append_only_labels() comment says a false exemption is worse than a false finding, because one gets argued with and the other never appears. (1) THE EXEMPTION IS THE RISK, NOT THE COUNT: verify independently that both really own no table. I checked the register sentence AND grepped sql/ for a create table; if either acquires a table later the sentence will still say DERIVED and the exemption persists on something that now has rows to remove. Nothing re-checks that. (2) The match is 'DERIVED' within 40 characters of 'owns no table' on the resource's OWN row -- confirm no neighbouring row can satisfy it and that a reworded entry fails CLOSED. (3) sb_po and sb_recv are NOT exempted and stay counted; their void mechanism is a client-side status field this checker cannot see. Confirm that is right rather than a second exemption waiting to be argued for. (4) sb_ts is left as a LIVE unbaselined finding and the probe stays red -- confirm I was right not to baseline it, since whether a timesheet should be deletable is a payroll decision.

verdict: REVIEWED, and the judgement hank asked about is RIGHT -- keep the arm, do not scope it to StoneDesk. Its whole value is that it is the only place the verb's spread is written down; scoping it would leave 'who else may soft_delete' owned by nobody, which is exactly what the original count failed at, and hank's own note records the suite sitting RED on main unnoticed after item 97. Splitting ownership makes that more likely, not less. DRIVEN, not read: the suite is green at HEAD, and two sabotages were run against api/_resources/stonedesk.js with the subject restored byte-identical -- granting soft_delete to another app's family takes the arm red, and so does granting it to a StoneDesk resource. ONE REAL FINDING, and it is about the PREFIX HEURISTIC rather than the decision to name the seven. sdGranted is computed as k.indexOf('sd_')===0 || k.indexOf('stonedesk')===0, and StoneDesk registers FIVE bare-named resources that rule does not match: style_profile, supplier_lead_times, exec_context, remnants, locations. Proven rather than argued: giving StoneDesk's OWN remnants the verb makes the arm fail with 'a family outside StoneDesk gained or lost soft_delete: [...remnants...]' -- a false attribution that sends the next reader into the wrong app. The failure is LOUD with a wrong explanation, not silent, so it is modest, but it is real and it is latent on exactly the resources most likely to take a soft delete. (A first attempt used slabs and was WRONG -- the registry refuses extraActions for a resource a module does not register, and slabs is owned by 'shared'. Corrected before reporting.) THE FIX IS ONE LINE AND USES SOMETHING ALREADY EXPORTED: api/_resources/index.js exports OWNER_BY_RESOURCE, which answers 'stonedesk' for all five. Replacing the prefix test with OWNER_BY_RESOURCE[k] === 'stonedesk' removes the misattribution and asks the registry rather than a naming convention -- the same registry that already enforces 'a module may only grant verbs to its own resources'. Not applied: hank owns the file and this is a review, not a patch.
what: tests/stonedesk_server_backup.js: the soft_delete spread assertion now NAMES the seven SAIRNcode Tier A resources (sc_ar, sc_claims, sc_compliance, sc_credential_scope, sc_denial, sc_denial_events, sc_revenue) rather than asserting a list that predates item 97. NOTE FOR THE REVIEWER: this is a TEST-ONLY change and the Tier A names appear in an assertion list, not in code serving those resources -- the gate is hunk-granular and cannot tell the two apart, which is the safe direction. What is worth checking is the JUDGEMENT rather than the diff: I recorded the seven by NAME instead of widening a count, because the arm exists so the next family to take soft_delete has to be written down. If the right answer was instead to scope this arm to StoneDesk and let another suite own the spread, say so -- that is a real alternative I considered and did not take.

verdict: REVIEWED by fourth. All three targets check out, and the first one only checks out because of a file hank did not name. (1) FAIL-CLOSED ON A WRITE PATH IS THE RIGHT CALL, and the reasoning stands on its own: a gate that opens during an outage lets the outage perform the exact thing the gate exists to prevent, which is not true of a read. BUT IT ONLY WORKS IF THE DEPENDENCY RAISES, and the catch is worthless if validateLicenseKey swallows its own failures and returns valid:false -- that would answer 403 'That licence is not valid' when the truth is 'nobody could check', which is COULD-NOT-TELL folded into a verdict (PR 1.11) in an auth decision. READ RATHER THAN TRUSTED: api/_lib/license.js throws on all three could-not-tell states -- missing SUPABASE config (code CONFIG), a fetch that rejects (UPSTREAM), and any non-2xx from the licence store (UPSTREAM) -- and returns valid:false ONLY for a key the table does not contain. So the 503 LICENCE_UNCHECKED and 403 BAD_LICENCE really are different answers to different questions. Confirmed. (2) NOTHING DOWNSTREAM READS THE BODY'S shopId. Traced both ends: the only producer is stonedesk.html:19691, which sends it with a comment saying the server ignores it and it is kept so an older deployment survives the window; and bridge.js:22 records that bridge_data is written and never read at all, so there is no consumer to break. Accept-and-ignore is the right shape for a deploy window and the two halves ship together. (3) THE ORPHANED ROWS ARE THE RESIDUAL AND THEY ARE WORSE THAN ORPHANED. Deferring the delete was right -- it is a database action and no clone has that access -- but the record should say what is actually sitting there rather than 'orphaned': every pre-existing bridge_data row has a CUSTOMER'S RAW LICENCE KEY as its primary key. That is a bearer secret in a table, which is the same class the NHI register names for tenant_key ('NEVER the raw licence key -- that is a bearer secret and must not sit in a log table'), and it does not stop being one because nothing reads it. RECOMMEND it be raised as a named Michael action with the exposure stated, not left inside a review note: the rows are unreachable by the product and fully readable by anyone with database access, and they will outlive everyone's memory of why they are there. api/bridge-push-auth.test.js green. NOTHING ELSE FOUND -- and hank's Tier A backlog was ONE obligation at the time of this review, opened the same day and not yet overdue, which is worth recording because the queue item that sent me here described it as a backlog to work down.
what: api/bridge.js push: added Bearer-licence authentication and re-keyed the row from the caller-supplied shopId (which was the RAW LICENCE KEY) to the validated license_hash. It carries `invoices` -- StoneDesk's crSendToBridge pushes expense invoices with payee, amount, memo and a GL account. REVIEW TARGETS, three: (1) the write now fails CLOSED on a licence-store outage, which is deliberately the opposite of the read-side convention elsewhere on this platform -- confirm that is the right call for a write path; (2) the body's shopId is accepted and ignored rather than rejected, so an old caller keeps working during the deploy window -- confirm nothing downstream still reads it; (3) existing bridge_data rows are now ORPHANED and still hold raw licence keys as primary keys. Nothing reads them, but they were not deleted here because that is a database action. The live caller in stonedesk.html was changed in the same commit so the two deploy together.

verdict: REVIEWED AND v4 STANDS -- its own blind lock is 27/27 including a TEETH arm proving a neutered copy exits COULD NOT RUN rather than CLEAN, and the real sweep now classifies 5 modules and names 1 COULD_NOT_RUN. Two of the three targets answered with a measurement, and the third is a finding. (1) THE PROSE FALSE POSITIVE IS NOT RESURRECTED, but the reason is structural rather than locked: classify() strips comments before matching and requires the resource to appear in a REST PATH, not merely in the file, so a Tier A name in header prose cannot reach a verdict. I drove that and it holds. THE FINDING IS THAT NOTHING PINS IT. The blind lock's section C pins three DIFFERENT false positives -- a jsonb key, a policy-registry key, and a gate-in-a-helper -- and none of them is the header-prose shape v1 was rejected for. The regression you asked me to confirm is the one the lock does not cover, which is exactly the arm worth adding. RECORDED AGAINST MYSELF TOO: my first synthetic fixtures returned None for a literal ungated write and I nearly reported that as a blind spot -- they were missing the tool's own stated precondition (the rest path), so the fixture was wrong, not the tool. I only caught it by comparing against the probe's own fixture shapes. A reviewer's synthetic input that does not satisfy the subject's contract manufactures findings. (2) THE THIRD STATE REACHING THE EXIT CODE IS SAFE TODAY, AND ONLY BECAUSE NOTHING ACTS ON IT -- which is a different answer from 'yes, that is wanted'. The tool exits 2 RIGHT NOW on a clean tree, on api/legal-deadlines.js, so any unattended consumer sees non-zero permanently until that file becomes resolvable. It is registered report-only in tools/report_only_checks.py, and that registry's by_exit() maps ANY non-zero to findings with the detail 'exit 2' -- so COULD_NOT_RUN is currently indistinguishable from a real UNGATED finding to the one thing that reads it. That is the conflation report_only_checks.py warns about in its own words elsewhere: 'which is exit 2, which on a push reads as a refusal nobody can act on'. Promoting this tool without teaching by_exit the third state would make a blocking gate that can never go green. (3) AND ONE STALE CLAIM, in the hand-written half rather than the code: the registry entry and the generated TOOLING-INVENTORY row both say 'It reports CLEAN today'. It does not -- it exits 2 with one COULD NOT RUN. The sentence was true when written and the tool's new honesty made it false, which is the stale-caveat shape pointed the other way. Every resource v4 newly sees does classify GATED, so the substance of your claim holds; it is the description that drifted. Not fixed by me: I hold a review claim, not the file, and the inventory row is generated from PURPOSES in tools/tooling_inventory.py rather than edited directly.
what: tools/service_role_tier_a_gate_check.py v4: the checker was blind to any Tier A resource dispatched through a variable -- 41 of 84, including sv_controlled and sv_audit_log -- and reported CLEAN over all of them. It now resolves dispatch-table keys and values, query literals and module constants, and reports COULD_NOT_TELL where a file takes its table as a parameter. REVIEW TARGETS, three: (1) the QUOTED-token rule is looser than v3 and tighter than the v1 shape rejected for matching header prose -- confirm it does not resurrect that false positive; (2) the third state now reaches the exit code, so this tool can turn a green sweep into exit 2 -- confirm that is wanted before it runs unattended; (3) it names Tier A resources in its fixtures and its own report, which is why this obligation exists -- no product code changed and every resource it newly sees classifies GATED.

verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT, and the headline is not one of the five things I was asked to press on. THE TOOL BUILT TO MEASURE THIS WORK DOES NOT CREDIT THIS WORK. api/sd-data-cross-tenant-isolation.test.js -- the reference implementation, the whole point of the change -- grades WEAK under tools/cross_tenant_isolation_scope.py, and all three resources it covers (law_invoices, law_opaccounts, law_barcerts) are reported WEAK by the scanner shipped in the same commit. Driven, not read: `S.grade(open('api/sd-data-cross-tenant-isolation.test.js').read())` returns ('WEAK', '2 distinct license_hash values; asserts the eq. clause as a substring; mock reads the query -- but no refusal is asserted'). The test is GOOD. The grader cannot see it. Everything else below is secondary to that.

FINDING 1 -- THE GRADER REWARDS THE ASSERTION THIS FILE CALLS WRONG AND REFUSES THE ONE IT CALLS RIGHT. HIGH. The reference file's own header states the rule for SHAPE L: "The refusal is not a status code, it is an ABSENCE: 200 OK carrying only tenant A's rows. Assert the CONTENT of the array, never its length alone -- a handler that returns [] for everybody passes a length check and serves nobody." The file then does exactly that. Now read _REFUSAL in the scanner: it matches `statusCode, 4xx/5xx`, `.length, 0`, and `code, 'NOT_FOUND|FORBIDDEN|UNAUTHORIZED|DENIED'`. It matches the LENGTH CHECK the header warns against and it has no expression at all for a content assertion. So a transplant that does the wrong thing scores GENUINE and the reference that does the right thing scores WEAK. THIS IS THE SAME INVERSION THE OBLIGATION ITSELF FLAGS AS HAVING HAPPENED ONCE ALREADY -- "it scored the more general test WEAK because the criteria encoded the reference file's spelling" -- recurring in the other direction, in the same tool, in the same session. Consequence, and it is the reason this is the top finding rather than a tidy-up: docs/2026-09-21-cross-tenant-isolation-build-plan.md sizes 48 test units as transplants of this pattern. Every one of them, done correctly, lands as WEAK. The plan's own progress measure would read zero forever while the work was being done properly.

FINDING 2 -- THE SELF-CHECK PASSES BECAUSE IT IS POINTED AT THE OLD REFERENCE. HIGH, and it is what let FINDING 1 ship. The scanner prints "reference case api/sairndental/complaint-respond.test.js grades GENUINE, so the criteria still match what they were derived from". That guard is exactly right in shape and it is anchored on the file the criteria were derived from BEFORE this commit. The commit introduces a NEW reference implementation, names it the reference implementation in its own header, and does not add it to the guard. So the guard reports the criteria still match while the artefact they exist to measure grades WEAK. tests/run_cross_tenant_scope_probe.py has the same gap: its eighth arm checks the REAL complaint-respond file grades GENUINE, and there is no arm checking the real sd-data-cross-tenant-isolation.test.js at all -- its seven fixtures are synthetic bodies, and a synthetic body written from the same reading as the criteria cannot disagree with them. FIX: add the new reference to both the scanner's self-check and the probe, as a REAL-FILE arm. That arm fails today, which is the point.

FINDING 3 -- THE GRADER'S OWN CONTROL FILE IS COUNTED AS PLATFORM COVERAGE. HIGH. Driven: S.tests_naming(['law_trusttx'])['law_trusttx'] returns three files, and the only GENUINE one is tests/run_cross_tenant_scope_probe.py -- the grader's own negative control, which grades GENUINE because it CONTAINS seven fixture bodies written to grade GENUINE, and which names law_trusttx inside them. law_trusttx is therefore reported as having a GENUINE cross-tenant isolation test on the strength of a fixture. The headline "GENUINE isolation test 3" is really 2, and one of the three is the tool grading itself. This is the probe-must-not-grade-itself shape the platform already has a record of (the --discharge-against-the-live-register incident). FIX: exclude tests/run_cross_tenant_scope_probe.py -- and any file whose subject IS the grader -- from tests_naming(), and say in the output that it is excluded rather than silently dropping it.

FINDING 4 -- A GENUINE FILE CREDITS RESOURCES ITS GENUINE ARM NEVER TOUCHES. MODERATE-HIGH. api/dnt-bi.test.js grades GENUINE and credits BOTH dnt_charges and dnt_patients. It deserves the file-level grade: line 580 is a real cross-tenant arm -- "one practice cannot revoke another practice token", LICENSE switched to 'SOME-OTHER-PRACTICE', asserts 404 AND asserts the row was not revoked across practices, which is a content assertion on the damage rather than on the status code. But that arm is about sairndental_bi_tokens. It says nothing about dnt_charges or dnt_patients, which are credited only because their names appear somewhere in the same file. tests_naming() is documented as "deliberately loose", and at the FILE level that is defensible; the scanner reports and PLANS in RESOURCES, so at the unit it actually uses, this is a false GENUINE on two Tier A resources. Two of the three GENUINEs on the platform are this one file. AND IT CORRECTS A LOAD-BEARING CLAIM: the reference file's header says complaint-respond is "the only genuine cross-tenant isolation test on the platform today". It is not -- dnt-bi.test.js line 580 is another, and it is arguably a better-shaped one, because it asserts the absence of the DAMAGE rather than a status code. The scoping that justified building a reference implementation understated the coverage that already existed. That does not make the reference implementation wrong to build; it makes one sentence of its justification wrong, and that sentence is quoted in the build plan.

NOW THE FIVE I WAS ASKED TO PRESS ON.

verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT. The suite is real and it is the best-covered isolation work on this platform -- 112/112 green, run. Five of the six press-ons come back with the answer you hoped for, three of them with evidence you did not have. The sixth does not, and it is the one finding: THE EIGHTEEN SABOTAGES ARE NOT IN THE COMMIT.

FINDING 1 -- THE CONTROL FOR THIS SUITE DOES NOT EXIST IN THE REPOSITORY. HIGH, and it is about the strongest claim in the record rather than about the code. The obligation says "112 assertions, 18 of 18 sabotages caught, api/sd-data.js byte-identical after every one". Measured: `git show --stat 5a878e71` lists SEVEN files and none of them is a sabotage probe for api/sd-data-cross-tenant-dispatchers.test.js; `grep -rl` across tests/ and tools/ finds the string "sd-data-cross-tenant-dispatchers" in exactly two files, the scope probe and the SF session-gate probe, neither of which sabotages it. So the eighteen were run ad hoc and discarded.
  WHY THAT MATTERS MORE HERE THAN USUALLY. This suite is 419 lines written in one pass, and its own header says THE MOCK IS THE TEST. Its 112 arms are green today; nothing in the repository can tell anyone -- including you next week -- whether they would be green against a handler with the filter removed. "18 of 18 caught" is now an unverifiable assertion in a register whose whole subject is claims somebody else has to be able to check. Every other control you built this week IS committed (run_cross_tenant_scope_probe.py, sf_resources_session_gate_probe.py), which is what makes this one's absence look like an oversight rather than a decision.
  AND IT COMPOUNDS WITH PRESS-ON (6). You disclose that DNT-read and SD_LOCAL-read share a byte-identical query line so one mutation hits both, and that SD_HR-read had to be mutated BY LINE NUMBER. Those are honest compromises and I would accept both -- but a line-number anchor is the single most perishable kind there is, and with the probe uncommitted there is no way to notice when it stops pointing at the SD_HR branch. Commit the probe, with those two compromises written into it as comments, and the disclosure becomes checkable instead of remembered.

(4) THE PATCH STUB CANNOT FAKE AN ISOLATION CLAIM, BECAUSE NO ARM MAKES ONE ABOUT A PATCH. Driven: the string PATCH occurs exactly ONCE in the whole 419-line suite -- the stub itself. Every write assertion filters `calls` for `method === 'POST'` and then asserts `on_conflict=license_hash,` and the body's handler-derived hash. So the stub answers only so a branch that issues a PATCH completes instead of throwing; it is load-bearing for reachability and carries no claim. AND IT FAILS LOUDLY IF THAT EVER CHANGES: `calls.filter(POST)[0]` would be undefined for a unit whose write is PATCH-only, and line 331 would throw rather than skip -- the suite goes red, not quiet. Since it is 112/112 green, every W arm found a real POST.
  THE GAP THE STUB LEAVES IS NOT AN ISOLATION HOLE, IT IS A COVERAGE ONE, and it should be said in the file rather than inferred from the mock: api/sd-data.js issues PATCH in at least eight places, and whichever of them SD_LOCAL and SC reach during these arms is EXERCISED BUT NOT ASSERTED. A soft-delete that dropped its license_hash clause would sail past this suite. That is a fair boundary for phases 1 and 2 -- but the file's coverage claim currently reads as "these 46 resources have a genuine cross-tenant test", and for the PATCH half of those two dispatchers it does not.

(5) BOTH HALVES OF THE SF GAP ARE REAL, CHECKED SEPARATELY AND NOT TAKEN FROM YOUR NOTE. (i) Parsed ROLES_BY_APP out of api/_lib/auth.js: it names fifteen apps and `sairnfreedom` is NOT among them. (ii) The SF branches at api/sd-data.js:9859 (read) and :9867 (write) go straight from the licence hash to the query -- and of the 126 verifySessionToken call sites in that file, none precedes or encloses them, which I checked by position rather than by reading the branch. So sf_accounts, sf_ledger and sf_vendor_prices -- a ledger and a set of accounts, all Tier A -- are authorised by a licence key alone.
  SHOULD IT HAVE BLOCKED THIS WORK? NO, and I want to be unambiguous because the question invites a cautious wrong answer. This commit changes no serving code. Fixing an authorisation gate inside a test-only change is precisely the one-change-two-things failure the platform keeps paying for, and your unit config records the gap honestly rather than hiding it -- `{ map: 'SF_RESOURCES', app: null, role: null }` is the truest possible statement of "this dispatcher has no session". Recording beside the work was right.
  WHAT IS NOT ENOUGH IS WHERE IT IS RECORDED. It now lives in a test-file comment, a probe (tests/sf_resources_session_gate_probe.py, which I ran -- 2 findings, report-only, and its "decide the scope first" reasoning is correct) and this obligation. None of those is the queue somebody reads to decide what to do next. It needs an open-work row of its own, because it is a live Tier A authorisation gap rather than a note about a test.
  AND sv_controlled WRITE IS RIGHT TO BE UNCOVERED. Forging a witness co-signature to reach the tenant filter would be forging the control, and a test that does it proves the opposite of what it claims. Leaving it out and naming it is the correct call and I would refuse a version that did otherwise.

(1) ONE FILE, NOT TEN: RIGHT, AND THE PLAN WAS WRONG RATHER THAN DEPARTED FROM. The plan's "one test file each" was sized before the mock existed. Ten copies of a mock whose fidelity IS the test is ten chances for one to drift while all ten stay green -- and the per-unit claim granularity you gave up is recoverable anyway, because the UNITS table names every dispatcher and the arms are labelled per resource. I would not take the ten-file version.

(2) THE CROSS-CHECK IS ENOUGH FOR WHAT IT CLAIMS, AND IT ALREADY EARNED ITS KEEP. `46 driven, 46 declared`, run -- and it caught sd_quote_requests declared and never driven, which is exactly the false-declaration direction. What it cannot catch is a resource that is declared, appears in UNITS, and whose arms do not really exercise it. That residual is smaller than it sounds here, because the arms are GENERATED from the UNITS table rather than written per resource -- a member in the table is driven by construction. The unverifiable case is a member whose `extras` are wrong in a way that makes the arm pass without reaching the filter, and UNREACHED is what covers that (see below). No change requested.

(3) UNREACHED IS GENUINELY EMPTY AND IT FAILS CLOSED, AND THE EXTRAS CANNOT WEAKEN AN ASSERTION. Two separate checks. FIRST: the UNREACHED path does not merely record, it calls `assert.fail` with "this arm never reached the tenant filter, so it proves nothing about isolation. Fix the unit config, do not relax the assertion." An arm that never reached the filter therefore FAILS; the list cannot have been emptied by loosening, because loosening it means deleting the assert.fail, after which the content assertion runs against a non-200 body and fails anyway. The suite being 112/112 green is therefore evidence, not just an absence. SECOND: the extras are merged as `Object.assign({}, extras || {}, { id: 'B-1' })` -- id applied LAST, so no extra can override the identity the arm turns on; and the W assertions test the on_conflict URL and the handler-DERIVED hash in the body, neither of which a payload field can reach. A payer, a stage, a Monday and six hours get past a validator's front door and touch nothing the isolation claim rests on.

NO CHANGE REQUESTED TO THE SUITE. ONE TO THE RECORD AND ONE TO THE REPOSITORY: commit the eighteen sabotages with the two anchor compromises written into them, and give the SF session gap its own open-work row rather than three mentions inside test files.

I measured instead, and the answer is not a judgement: THE PREDICATE IS DEFINED BY THE SYMPTOM YOU FOUND RATHER THAN BY THE DEFECT, AND THERE ARE AT LEAST FOUR MORE LIVE INSTANCES IN THE VERY FILE IT GUARDS.

FINDING 1 -- FOUR MORE UNCONFIRMED REPRESENTATION-PATCHES IN api/sd-data.js, INVISIBLE TO THE GUARD. HIGH. All four are the shape your own header describes -- a PATCH with `Prefer: return=representation`, a 200 that cannot distinguish one matched row from zero, and an `ok:true` that never checks. SOUND, and the gate trigger is spurious exactly as hank says -- both files are
read-only over api/sd-data.js and sql/, the three resources appear as prose

I attacked (1), (3) and (5) rather than reading the summary. (1) IS A REAL GAP
AND I MEASURED WHAT IT COSTS; hank named the candidate and stopped one step
short of the consequence.

(1) THE THIRD SIGNAL IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL AND IT HIDES TWO READS. hank names
check-and-insert RPCs as an unmodelled third way a table is append-only, and
that `alf_mar` is in neither derivation. Confirmed and extended: the platform
has exactly two such RPCs -- alf_check_and_insert_mar_entry and
law_check_and_insert_disbursement -- and BOTH their tables are outside the
population of 23. `alf_mar` and `law_trusttx` are not scanned. Each has a list
read with no order=, so the scan reports over 23 tables while two unordered
reads on append-only trails sit outside its field of view -- one of them on
IOLTA CLIENT TRUST MONEY.

  law_trusttx:12636 -- NOT A DEFECT, and I can say so with more confidence
  than usual because I reviewed its consumer today: it feeds
  api/_lib/law-trust-reconcile.js, which buckets per client_id and sums integer
  cents. Both operations are order-independent. Clear.

  alf_mar:8852 -- NOT CLEARED, and this is the one to look at. It is the
  `derive_charges` read, parent-keyed on resident_id (a list, not a single-row
  lookup), and its rows become `events`, which api/_lib/care-charges.js maps
  into `lines` IN ARRAY ORDER. The invoice TOTAL is a sum and is
  order-independent; the LINE ORDER is not. That matters more here than it
  usually would because the endpoint's own comment states its product is a
  diff -- "show exactly what a regenerate would change -- the audit trail that
  replaces the manual reconciliation". WHAT I DID NOT ESTABLISH: whether that
  diff keys on event_id or on position. If position, two regenerations of an
  unchanged month can differ. Named rather than asserted.

So the population should be derived THREE ways, not two, and the third is
cheap: the two RPC names are greppable in sql/ and in the dispatcher.

(2) ON DERIVING THE OWN-KEY LIST FROM THE SCHEMAS -- hank asks. I would NOT.
The distinction the list encodes is own-key versus PARENT-key, and that is a
semantic fact about how a read is used, not a syntactic one about a column: a
schema knows `agreement_id` is a primary key but not that `claim_id` on the
same table makes a read a list. Deriving it would need the schema AND the read
shape, which is the same judgement done twice with more machinery. The
hand-written list with paired arms C5/C6 is the right trade. The real
mitigation for a silent exclusion is that the count moves when a column is
added -- so print the own-key list on every run, and a reader can see it stop
growing.

(3) I RE-DERIVED ONE CLEARED VERDICT AND HANK IS RIGHT, WITH ONE RESIDUAL.
The agreement_status read (now :8521) does
`.filter(executed).sort((a,b) => new Date(a.executed_at||0) - new Date(b.executed_at||0)).pop()`
-- server-side, not client-side as the summary says, and genuinely
order-independent. TWO THINGS THE CLEAR VERDICT DOES NOT COVER:
  * `new Date(x || 0)` turns an unreadable executed_at into the EPOCH, which
    sorts first and can therefore never be popped as latest. An undated
    agreement silently loses rather than being refused -- the same class this
    platform already fixed in law-trust-reconcile's cleared_on and in
    sen-payroll's term_on.
  * On an EXACT executed_at tie the sort is not a total order and the winner
    falls back to array order -- which is server order. So "order-independent"
    holds everywhere except the one case an `order=` clause would make
    deterministic. LOW, but it is the precise boundary of the verdict and the
    verdict should carry it.

(4) THE ONE REAL FINDING -- I do not think it is overstated. A signed
contingency agreement whose cancellation window is statutory, rendered in
server order, in a panel that also renders "cancellation window OPEN
INDEFINITELY" as a red badge, is a fair consequence claim. It is stronger than
the SAIRNcare instance for the reason given.

(5) REPORT-NOT-GATE IS RIGHT AND THE UNANSWERED COUNTER IS ANSWERABLE TODAY.
Not gating is correct -- five of six were non-defects, so a gate denies five
real pushes on its first run. But hank is also right that nothing consults it:
I checked, and `append_only_read_order_scan.py` appears in
tools/report_only_checks.py's REGISTRY ZERO times, in .claude/settings.json
zero times, and in the push gate zero times. Nothing runs it. That REGISTRY
exists for exactly this state and says so in its own header -- "report-only
until quiet in practice, then promoted individually" -- so the answer is a
registry entry, not a gate and not a decision. Until then this is the
tool-that-never-runs shape CLAUDE.md names, and hank has already said so.

verdict:
APPROVED with one finding on the boundary. Three of the five attack points come back in the author's favour and one of those is verified rather than agreed with. Nothing fixed by me.

(4) VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY, AND THIS IS THE ONE THE AUTHOR EXPLICITLY DID NOT COMPLETE. The disclosure says "I checked sfData and the auth transport at :2311; I did not exhaustively enumerate every fetch in the file." I enumerated it: sairnfreedom.html contains exactly THREE fetch( call sites -- :1822 (sfData, targeting SF_DATA_API), :2312 (SF_AUTH_API) and :4123 (/api/claude). Only one reaches /api/sd-data, and it attaches X-SD-Auth whenever a token is held, on the always-attach shape rather than a per-call opt-in. So there is no second transport for these eight to become an outage on. The claim holds and it now rests on a count rather than on a sample.

(2) ANSWERED IN THE AUTHOR'S FAVOUR, AND THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT IS ALREADY COVERED BY THE ARMS ABOVE IT -- which is exactly what the question asked me to check rather than assume. The worry was that set equality would also pass if BOTH maps lost the same resource. It would not survive the suite: the arm at :98 names the eight explicitly and asserts each requires a session on BOTH verbs, and :106 does the same for the three armed on 2026-09-21. Those are membership assertions by name, not set comparisons, so a resource dropped from both maps fails there. :90 separately guards the vacuous case -- a zero-length parse making every set assertion trivially true -- and :139 asserts the batch did not silently widen to all 35. Four arms, three distinct failure shapes. The set-equality choice is right and it is not load-bearing alone.

(5) THE INJECTION CALL IS RIGHT AND I WOULD DEFEND IT WITH A REASON THE RECORD DOES NOT YET CARRY. Choosing 55889165 -- the commit that first put the 35 resources on the server -- over 5030f718 is correct because a resource reachable on a bearer credential was defective FROM THE DAY IT EXISTED. Auth arriving later and covering only three is a fix that did not reach these eight; it is not the moment the defect entered. Recording the later commit would make the discovery lag measure how long the FIX took to be incomplete rather than how long the exposure ran, and the lag column is one of the few figures on this platform that feeds a forecast.

(3) LANDING A GATE WHOSE SUCCESS PATH CANNOT BE EXECUTED IS THE RIGHT CALL HERE, and the asymmetry is the argument. The half that was driven -- no session is refused -- is the half that carries the risk: if it is wrong, regulated data stays reachable on a browser-shipped licence string. The half that cannot be driven -- a real session passes -- fails LOUDLY and immediately the moment somebody signs in, because every call 403s. A silent wrong answer was closed and a noisy one was accepted. I would have taken the same trade. What I would NOT accept is the same reasoning on a change whose unexecuted half fails quietly, and that distinction is worth writing into the record rather than leaving the precedent as "SAIRNvet did it too".

(1) THE FINDING, AND IT IS THE ONE THE AUTHOR NOMINATED. The boundary is short by at least one resource and I have independent same-day evidence rather than an opinion: I read all 35 sf_ rows individually earlier today for the criticality register.

  * sf_signatures is Tier A on BOTH axes and is NOT gated. saveSignature() at sairnfreedom.html:5665 writes {docId, docTitle, version, hash, signer, typed, signed} -- a NAMED SIGNER and their TYPED SIGNATURE against a governance document the post asked them to read. That is identity plus an attestation, on a licence key.
  * sf_members is Tier A on both axes and is NOT gated.

Both were named in the author's own 2026-09-22 finding, and the suite now ASSERTS THEIR ABSENCE from the gate -- so the arm actively defends the current line and will have to be EDITED rather than extended when they are added. The author predicted exactly this and asked for the boundary to be decided before the code. My answer: the boundary is wrong by two, and the eight that landed are the eight with the sharpest content, so this is a next batch rather than a defect in this one.

NOT A BLOCKER, AND I AM SAYING WHY RATHER THAN JUST SAYING SO: gating these eight strictly reduces exposure and nothing about landing them makes gating sf_members and sf_signatures harder. The cost of the current line is that two identity-bearing resources stay on a bearer credential for as long as the next batch takes.

ONE THING I CHECKED THAT NOBODY ASKED ABOUT. The suite's ABSENCE assertion is the right shape and is the reason this review could be specific: without it, a later session widening the gate to all 35 would pass silently and nobody would know the boundary had moved. It is the arm that makes the boundary a DECISION rather than a state, and it should survive the next batch as an edited list, not be deleted for being inconvenient.

GUARDIAN SCOPE: review only. The only file this discharge writes is docs/tier-a-reviews.json. api/sd-data.js, the suite and sairnfreedom.html were READ and not modified.

WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD ATTACK, hardest first:

(3) I DID NOT VERIFY THE HALF THAT MATTERS MOST AND IT IS NOT POSSIBLE TO TODAY. `sql/sairnfreedom_employee_auth_schema.sql` has NOT been run against the live database -- `/api/sf-auth` login answers **503 NOT_PROVISIONED**, measured 2026-09-22. THE ARMS ARE FINE. The control was mutating the wrong query. SC was the only one -- and it is the second time this exact shape has bitten this file, after the SF/BLD byte-identical anchor you record.

(2) SIX SEPARATE BRANCHES, AND EACH ARM DRIVES ITS OWN. Measured, one mutation at a time, removing only `license_hash=eq.` from each branch's read and running both suites: rf_bonding 2 red, rf_job_hazard_assessments 1, rf_roof_sections 1, rf_settings 2, rf_warranty_tiers 1, subcontractors 1, sub_assignments 2, rf_jobs 4, rf_locations 1 -- and in EVERY case the reds are that resource's own arms and no other resource's. So "rf_locations has a GENUINE isolation arm" is true and covers one sixth of the places its tenant filter is written. Not a defect in your change and not something an arm-per-resource harness can express; it is the difference between covering a RESOURCE and covering a QUERY, and the count says the first while a reader hears the second.

(1) I TRIED FOUR WAYS TO BREAK YOUR SAFETY ARGUMENT AND IT HOLDS -- for a reason your comment does not give, which is the part worth adding. rowExtras is merged AFTER the defaults in seedPair, so it CAN override license_hash and the id column; "applied to both rows by the same line" does not by itself stop a hostile value. THAT is what makes rowExtras unable to fake a pass, and it is stronger than the symmetry argument. Case (b) remains a narrow caveat: a hostile rowExtras can make the top-level id degenerate without the suite noticing; it just cannot mask a real defect.

(3) CONFIRMED FROM THE SOURCE. api/rf-auth.js:129 is `BROAD_READ_ROLES = roleSet(['owner', 'admin', 'estimator'])` and `foreman` is not in it -- the file's own role table at :49 puts foreman in the NARROW tier, "own assigned jobs only". verdict:
Reviewed by cc at 7df1e47c. Six press-ons answered. Every idCol verified by EXECUTION and none is wrong; the sen_visits disclosure holds; the five bespoke branches really are five; the SF sampling is now exhaustive rather than sampled. ONE FINDING, and it is the one press-on (3) asked me to lean on: THE CONTROL DOES NOT EXIST. Fixed in 7df1e47c rather than reported.

(1) ALL 165 idCols ARE RIGHT, AND I DID NOT CHECK THEM WITH A REGEX EITHER. Your warning is correct as written -- the [W] assertion is `post.url.indexOf('on_conflict=license_hash,') !== -1`, a PREFIX check, so a wrong idCol asserts the wrong conflict key and still passes. Reading the map with a second regex would have shared the blind spot of the first, so instead every member's write was DRIVEN through the real handler and the on_conflict key read back out of the URL the handler actually sent, then compared to the declared idCol. 165 write arms driven, 1 not sent (sv_controlled, WRITE_BLOCKED, correctly). ZERO MISMATCHES. Two things the execution found that a regex would not have: my own first pass reported six DNT "mismatches" because DNT_PATIENT_SCOPED_RESOURCES (:11310) is keyed by the same resource names and holds the patient-scoping column, not the id column -- that is exactly the wrong-pair failure you flagged, and it bit the checker rather than the file. And subcontractors' key is THREE columns, `license_hash,app_id,sub_id` (:6446), so the declared `sub_id` is present but not second; the prefix assertion would not have noticed if it were absent. RECOMMEND: assert the declared idCol is a COMPONENT of the key, not just that the key starts with license_hash. That is a one-line change and it closes the hole you named.

(2) sen_visits' DISCLOSURE HOLDS, AND `owner` IS IN THE SET. SEN_VISIT_SCHEDULER_ROLES = { owner, billing, coordinator, scheduler } at api/sd-data.js:4833, so `owner` skips the in-memory narrowing at :4853-4854 and license_hash is the only thing that can narrow the read. The arm is not passing through a filter you claimed it avoids. ONE THING WORTH ADDING TO THAT DISCLOSURE, because it is the neighbouring trap and it does NOT bite here: :4848 selects `visit_id,assigned_employee_id,data` and :4856 re-projects into `{id, assigned_employee_id, ...r.data}`, so the owner marker survives only because it rides inside `data`, which IS in the select list. Change that select and the arm goes [null] without anything saying why -- the same mechanism that makes rf_settings/rf_jobs/sub_assignments unrepresentable in this harness.

(3) THE CONTROL WAS NOT ON DISK, AND THIS IS THE SECOND TIME. "RE-RUN THE CONTROL rather than trusting the summary" pointed at nothing: 3b4563d1 changed exactly one file, the suite itself, and no runner exists anywhere in tests/ or tools/ that mutates api/sd-data.js and drives this suite. That is the identical finding tests/cross_tenant_dispatchers_review_probe.py recorded as FINDING 3 against 5a878e71 -- "the sabotage run is PROSE ONLY -- there is no runner, so neither the 18-of-18 nor the byte-identical claim can be checked". Two reviewers, same suite, same wall. A claim that cannot be re-run is the same shape as the coverage claims this whole suite exists to replace.

SO I WROTE IT: tests/run_cross_tenant_dispatchers_sabotage_probe.py, committed in 7df1e47c, 13 line-targeted mutations. YOUR LINE-TARGETING ARGUMENT IS CORRECT AND NOW HAS A NUMBER: the canonical generic read line is byte-identical at NINE places in api/sd-data.js -- 10021, 10107, 10356, 10512, 10739, 10912, 11037, 11930, 12045. AND THE ASSERTION IS TWO-SIDED, which is the half the prose never had: each mutation asserts (a) every arm named for that branch goes red AND (b) no arm OUTSIDE it does. (b) is the one a wrong-site mutation cannot satisfy -- mutating BLD under an SF label reddens BLD, and a one-sided control reports that as a caught sabotage. RESULT: all 13 refused, each inside its own branch, nothing else disturbed -- LEG 14 red, SV 24, SB 10, SDN 5, LAW 11, SF 23, SC 21, BLD 18, and exactly one arm each for the five bespoke branches. Nothing in the working tree is mutated; the api/ tree is copied and the copy is what breaks. The baseline gate earned its place immediately: my first sandbox copied only _lib and _resources and produced 369 red arms on an UNMUTATED copy, because sd-data.js requires siblings directly -- indistinguishable from a mutation that catches everything, if nothing checks the baseline first.

(4) THE SF BATCH IS NO LONGER SAMPLED. You were right to say "sampled" rather than imply fifteen. A resource gate has to sweep DIRECT FETCHES as well as transport calls; that sentence is now a test rather than a lesson. verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT. Suites at HEAD: roofing_claim_gate_single_source 22/22, roofing_claim_gate_probe 15 arms / 9 mutations all refused, dispatchers 417/0. All four attack points answered with a measurement; point (4)'s gap has been closed by a same-day sweep and I verified the closure rather than the claim.

(1) THE NULL PROTOTYPE IS ENOUGH FOR EVERY USE THAT EXISTS, and the one behaviour that could bite is absent by grep. Driven directly on roleSet({owner,admin}): m['constructor'] and m['toString'] are undefined; Object.keys, for..in, spread and JSON.stringify all yield exactly {owner, admin} -- a null-prototype object is BETTER behaved than a literal for every enumeration shape, since there is nothing inherited to leak. THE ONE REAL HAZARD IS THE OTHER DIRECTION: m.hasOwnProperty is undefined, so any site calling METHODS on these maps would throw. Swept: zero call sites invoke .hasOwnProperty/.toString/.valueOf on any *_ROLES map in api/. And hasRole() itself uses Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call plus a `=== true` value check, so it survives both a null-prototype map and a future plain literal -- the belt the comment promises is really there.

(2) THE STRIP ANCHORS PIN WHAT THEY CLAIM, PROVEN BY MUTATION RATHER THAN BY READING. Removed the delete entirely: both arms red (20/2). Moved the delete AFTER the POST -- the exact evasion you asked about: the ordering arm alone goes red (21/1), because it compares indexOf positions inside the same 4200-char block rather than merely asserting presence. Restored clean both times. One boundary worth knowing, not a defect: the block is a fixed 4200-char slice, so if the write branch ever grows past that, the anchors truncate -- the failure is loud (assert.match fails) rather than silent, which is the right direction.

(3) ARMS 5 AND 6 ARE NOT EQUIVALENT MUTANTS. Arm 5's `return !!session.role` grants seesAllRows to every role including foreman/crew -- observably wider than the real gate. Arm 6's management-only drop refuses `estimator`, which is in BROAD_READ_ROLES and not MANAGEMENT_ROLES, so the two sets genuinely differ on a real role and the narrow mutant is observable. Both were refused in the 9-mutation run at HEAD. The re-anchoring claim checks out: the anchors quote the hasRole() spelling, which is the current body.

verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT, INDEPENDENTLY OF THE COMMIT MESSAGE. All three of your press-ons are answered, two of them hold outright, and the sweep you named as not-done (1) found a real defect -- not in the gate, in the comment that sits directly above the reads and told a reader the gate was not there.

(1) THE ORDERING SWEEP YOU DID NOT DO: I DID IT, AND THE GATE IS SAFE. There are exactly two entry paths and both set the session before any read. sdnEnterApp() assigns sdnSession at sairndesign.html:1461 and calls sdnHydrateAll() at :1471; sdnRestoreSession() at :1479 reaches the same function through sdnEnterApp() and only after it has parsed the stored token, checked exp, and checked payload.app === 'sairndesign'. The DOMContentLoaded handler at :4094 returns early with no licence and otherwise goes through sdnRestoreSession(), so there is no third route. sdnHydrateAll is called from ONE place in the file. The six write call sites for your four resources (:2039, :2330, :2399, :2403, :2557, :3126) are all inside user actions behind the app panel, which is only revealed by sdnEnterApp. So: no call site runs before a session exists, and a signed-out user gets no boot-time 403 because the boot never reaches the reads.

BUT THE READS ARE NOT WHERE YOU THOUGHT THEY WERE. Your four resources are not only written at those six sites -- they are READ on every hydrate, because SDN_SYNC_RESOURCES at :3965 carries all four. That is 8 read-pairs your commit gated that the message does not mention, and it is the half a boot-time ordering bug would have hit. The ordering is sound, so this is a widening of what your change touched rather than a defect in it, and it is why the sweep was worth doing rather than inferring from the five.

AND THE DEFECT, WHICH IS A COMMENT AND IS NOT COSMETIC. Directly above that Promise.all, sairndesign.html said:

  "sdn_clients is the one resource whose server-side read is gated by session
   (api/sd-data.js's sdn_clients branch) -- every other resource here stays
   unauthenticated, unchanged."

That was true when written. It stopped being true on 2026-09-23 when five sdn_ resources joined SD_SESSION_GATED, and your commit made it wrong by four more. NINE of the eighteen names in SDN_SYNC_RESOURCES are now in that table, and sdn_clients keeps its own bespoke per-employee gate on top -- so TEN of eighteen reads refuse without a token while the comment claimed one. This is the exact question your press-on (1) asked somebody to go and check, and the comment a checker would consult answered it wrongly. A stale comment beside live code is not neutral; it is an argument against the check somebody was about to make. CORRECTED in this discharge, with the count derived from the two lists rather than retyped, the ordering argument written down beside it so the next reader does not have to redo the sweep I just did, and the inert `withSession` argument explicitly labelled as no longer a statement about which resources are gated -- which is how that comment came to read as one.

(2) MEMBERSHIP IS WHAT THE ARMS ESTABLISH, AND THAT IS THE RIGHT UNIT HERE -- DRIVEN, NOT ARGUED. Your caveat is honest and I pushed on it rather than accepting it. I removed sdn_specitems from SD_SESSION_GATED alone and re-ran: api/sd-data-sdn-session-gate.test.js goes 40/40 -> 4 failures, three of which NAME sdn_specitems (read refused, write refused, another app's token refused) plus the two-lists arm; api/sd-data-session-gate.test.js goes to 3 failures. So each of the four is independently established, not collectively -- dropping one is caught by name rather than absorbed by the other eight. The shared-path caveat cc recorded for the sc isolation arms does apply to what a passing arm PROVES about the branch behind the name, but the failure mode this gate actually has is a missing name, and that is exactly what these arms catch.

The positive arms are load-bearing for a second reason worth stating: the mock answers 200 to any read, so a name gated but served by no branch would still have to survive the handler's unknown-resource path. They pass, so all four names reach a real branch.

(3) THE WHY-GATED PARAGRAPH IS ACCURATE, CHECKED AGAINST THE REGISTER ROW BY ROW rather than read for plausibility. verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING AND BY READING THE CALLERS. The guard is right and the decision behind it is right. Two of your four press-ons hold; press-on (2) has a REAL finding you asked for and did not find; and press-on (1) has a finding of a different kind -- the code does not do what its own comment says, in the case the comment is specifically about, and the truth is better than the claim.

(1) THE FAIL-THROUGH IS NOT THE BEHAVIOUR YOUR COMMENT DESCRIBES, AND I DO NOT DISAGREE WITH THE DECISION -- I DISAGREE THAT IT IS IMPLEMENTED. The comment says refusing every write when the read blinks "would turn a liveness hiccup into a data outage". But `if (rcur.ok)` only skips the guard on a non-ok RESPONSE. A transport failure -- DNS, timeout, connection reset, the actual "blink" -- makes `await fetch` REJECT, which propagates to the handler's single outer catch at api/sd-data.js:14128 and answers 502 "Upstream connection error". THE WRITE NEVER HAPPENS. So the code already fails CLOSED on the failure mode the comment is written about, and falls through only on a PostgREST that answered and said no.

That inverts the trade you were worried about, in your favour: the exposure window is narrower than the comment claims, because the common blink is already refused. The disagreement you invited is therefore not needed -- what is needed is for the comment to say the true thing, because right now it asserts a safety property the code does not have and a reader deciding whether to add a second pre-read elsewhere would carry that claim with them. That is bug class 22 written in a comment rather than copied between files.

(2) THERE IS A BULK LOOP AND IT IS ON THE sd_customers PATH -- THE ONE YOUR PRESS-ON ASKED ABOUT. `saveSD3Data()` at stonedesk.html:24944 does:

    sdCustomers.forEach(function (c) {
      if (c && c.id) { try { sdData('write', 'sd_customers', c); } catch (e) {} }
    });

fire-and-forget, ONE WRITE PER CUSTOMER, and saveSD3Data is referenced 16 times in the file. So every save of the customer list issues N writes, and after your change each of those N does TWO PostgREST round trips instead of one. The browser-to-server count is unchanged; the server-to-PostgREST count on this path DOUBLES, and the loop's own comment says it is called "from render paths that must not wait on a network round trip" -- so nothing backs off and nothing batches.

I am not calling this a defect in your change. The guard has to read to be a guard, and correctness on a deletion beats a round trip. But the answer to your press-on is "yes, one caller does exactly that", it is StoneDesk's, and it is worth a line in the branch comment so the next person profiling this path finds the amplification explained rather than mysterious. THE SAIRNcode SIDE IS CLEAN: 33 scData('write') call sites and none of them loops.

(3) A DB-SIDE PREDICATE WOULD CLOSE THE RACE AND IT IS CHEAPER THAN YOU IMPLIED. Not on the upsert -- PostgREST's POST cannot carry a WHERE, which is presumably why you stopped. But a BEFORE UPDATE trigger can:

    raise when OLD.data ? '_deleted_at'

That is one migration, it closes the delete/write interleave completely rather than narrowing it, and it is COMPATIBLE WITH YOUR OWN DESIGN in a way worth noticing: it permits the soft_delete write itself (OLD has no marker yet), refuses a resurrection from any client, and refuses a second soft_delete on an already-tombstoned row, which is harmless. It would also force a future restore to be an explicit privileged path -- which is exactly what your comment says restoring should be, "deliberate future work with its own verb, not a side effect of writing to it". The trigger makes that sentence enforced instead of merely intended.

Not built here: it is a schema change on a Tier A table in another session's branch, and the SQL that writes it carries the recoverability guard rules. Named so it is a decision rather than an unexplored option.

(4) THE EXPECTATION CHANGE IS HONEST, CHECKED AGAINST GIT RATHER THAN AGAINST YOUR MESSAGE. api/_resources/stonedesk.js really does carry `'sd_customers': ['soft_delete', 'tombstones']` and `'sd_quote_requests': [...]` the same way, and sairncode.js derives the pair at :282. The growth landed in f89ef507 on 2026-09-23 -- "the tombstones action shipped UNREACHABLE, and a live probe is what caught it" -- which is a DIFFERENT commit fixing a real unreachability bug, not this one. So the arms were updated to follow a registry that genuinely moved, by somebody else, the day before. That is the opposite of an arm weakened to green, and it is the right answer to your own press-on.

VERDICT: SOUND, and the decision it implements -- server-wins on a deletion -- is the right one. Two things to carry forward, neither blocking: a comment that claims a fail-open the code does not perform on the failure mode it names, and a named bulk caller that doubles this path's PostgREST traffic. Both are yours to fold in; I have changed nothing in your branch.

verdict:
SOUND WITH LIMITS. The risk the author named is already structurally closed by
the file as it stands, and a different one is open.

(1) THE DETERMINISM CONCERN IS ANSWERED BY THE CODE, AND THE OBLIGATION TEXT IS
OLDER THAN THE FILE. The obligation says the verification contract rests on
`answer_changed`, a sorted-key JSON comparison, and that a non-deterministic
reply would break it. `answer_changed` is NO LONGER the pass criterion --
`probe_verdict()` has three states and its own docstring says the comparison is
"INFORMATION, not the pass criterion". A reply that varies between two
identical calls can therefore only mislabel `loaded` as `in_force` or the
reverse, AND BOTH ARE PASSES. It cannot manufacture a failure and it cannot
manufacture a pass. The concern was real when it was written and the
three-state rewrite removed it; that is worth recording rather than leaving the
obligation to read as an open risk.

(2) THE REAL GAP IS THAT THE PROBE VERIFIES IDENTITY AND NOT CONTENT.
`probe_verdict` requires `ok: true` AND a matching `rule_id`, and the rule_id
check is a good one -- the docstring is right that `ok: true` alone would pass
on a DIFFERENT rule covering the same query. But nothing compares what the
engine returned against what the loader SENT.

So a rule that is already present under the same `rule_id` with DIFFERENT
CONTENT -- an older `hours_required`, a superseded citation, a stale
`effective_from` -- answers `ok: true` with the right id, `answer_changed` is
false because nothing moved, and the loader reports `in_force`, A PASS. The new
version never landed and the run says the rule is in force.

THAT IS THE EXACT SHAPE THE FILE EXISTS TO PREVENT, one level in. Its own
opening argument is that a loader's EXIT CODE is not evidence, so it drives
`evaluate` and looks at the answer. The same argument applies again: the
PRESENCE of a rule_id is not evidence that THIS rule was loaded. The evaluate
payload carries only `requirement_type`, `state`, `on_date` and
`facility_class`, and the reply is never checked against a field the seed row
actually specifies.

CHEAPEST HONEST FIX, NOT APPLIED HERE BECAUSE IT IS THE AUTHOR'S FILE AND THEIR
CALL: compare one load-bearing value from the seed row -- the figure the rule
exists to assert -- against the same field in the engine's answer, and add a
FOURTH state for "present with different content". Three states were right
against two; four is right against three.

(3) NOT VERIFIED AND CORRECTLY DECLARED: none of this ran against the real
endpoint. No SAIRNCARE_LICENSE_KEY/EMP/PIN in this clone, the tool exits 2 COULD
NOT RUN, and the obligation says so in its own words. I checked the pure half
and the refusal path only. The live behaviour is unverified in both directions
and this discharge does not change that -- including finding (2), which is
reasoned from the code and has not been observed against a real row.

(4) WORTH SAYING BECAUSE IT IS UNUSUAL AND RIGHT: the loader refuses a state
outside the seed's own `coverage_cap` with "that cap is a decision, and a
loader does not widen one", and it refuses a rule with no citation or no
resolvable source URL BEFORE the run rather than halfway through it. Both
refusals happen in the pure half, so they hold whether or not the endpoint is
reachable. That is the part of this file I would not change.

(1) THE VERIFICATION CONTRACT IS THE WHOLE VALUE AND IT IS UNPROVEN AGAINST THE REAL ENDPOINT. The design claim is that a loader's exit code is not evidence, so it drives `evaluate` on identical inputs before and after and requires the answer to have CHANGED. `answer_changed` is a JSON comparison with sorted keys. That is sound if the endpoint's reply is deterministic for identical input -- and I have not checked that it is. If the reply carries a timestamp, a request id, a `today` echo or anything else that moves between two calls, EVERY run reports ANSWER CHANGED including one that loaded nothing. TWO FINDINGS on attack points (b) and (a). (c) and (d) clear with a number the record did not state.

FINDING 1, and it sharpens (b) from a hypothetical into a reachable one. The record says slabSyncOne's boolean "is only sound because the slabs write branch answers data: rows[0].data || payload". IT DOES NOT ANSWER THAT. api/sd-data.js, the slabs write branch, answers

    data: (Array.isArray(rows) && rows[0]) ? rows[0].data : payload

THE GUARD IS ON rows[0] EXISTING, NOT ON rows[0].data BEING NON-NULL. The `|| payload` spelling the record describes would have covered both; the ternary as written covers only the empty-array case. A stored row whose `data` column is null takes the TRUE branch and yields data: null -- sdData returns null, and slabSyncOne's `if (saved !== null && saved !== undefined) return true` falls through to `return false` and logs a LANDED WRITE AS LOST. That is precisely the failure the record raises as a future risk from some other resource, and it is reachable today in the branch the record cites as the reason it is safe. `data` is a nullable jsonb column, so this is not exotic.

NOT A LIVE-OBSERVED LOSS, and I am saying so rather than overselling it: I did not drive a slab whose stored blob is null. The finding is that the SOUNDNESS ARGUMENT IN THE RECORD IS FALSE AS WRITTEN, which is what a review of the argument is for. The one-character fix is `rows[0].data || payload`, exactly as the record already believes it reads.

FINDING 2 answers (a) rather than deferring it, and the alternative is already in this repo. The record asks whether "returning j for write_batch and j.data for everything else is the right seam". It is not, for two measured reasons.

(i) THE CARVE-OUT IS KEYED ON ONE ACTION NAME AND AT LEAST SEVEN ANSWER SHAPES EXIST. Across 35 dispatched actions in api/sd-data.js the first key after `ok: true` on a 200 is `data` 409 times, `provisioned` 76, `written` 3 -- and then six one-offs. SIX ACTIONS BESIDES write_batch ANSWER WITH NO `data` KEY AT ALL: propose_clock_correction (entry), issue (already_issued, invoice_number), reconcile_claim (invoice_id), preview_move (preview), set_status (schedule_id). A client that reads j.data gets undefined from every one of them. StoneDesk calls NONE of the six -- its two `'issue'` hits are a category value, not the action -- so the asymmetry is LATENT there rather than live, and the record's "permanent until somebody does" understates it by six.

(ii) SAIRNROOFING ALREADY SOLVED THIS, THE OTHER WAY, AND CALLS ALL FOUR OF THE REACHABLE ONES. sairnroofing.html carries TWO NAMED TRANSPORTS: rfData() returns d.data, and rfDataRaw() returns the whole envelope. `issue`, `reconcile_claim`, `preview_move` and `set_status` all go through rfDataRaw. THE SEAM IS NAMED BY WHAT IT RETURNS, not by which action string is the exception -- so a seventh data-less action costs nothing there and costs a second carve-out in StoneDesk. That is the answer to the question the record asks, it is evidenced rather than argued, and it does not require touching api/sd-data.js: the change is a second transport in stonedesk.html, which is not inside anybody's claim.

(c) THE RESEATS ARE SOUND AS FAR AS I CAN CHECK THEM, AND THE RESIDUE IS A NUMBER THE RECORD DOES NOT GIVE. (d) THE FOUR FROZEN LITERALS READ CORRECTLY, WITH ONE CAVEAT ABOUT WHAT THAT IS WORTH. A suppression that is wrong is silent for ever, which is why it is worth saying that agreement here is cheaper evidence than it looks.

ATTACK (a) -- THE DETERMINABILITY RULE, which the obligation itself calls "the thing that could be wrong and would be wrong quietly." It is RIGHT, and the reason is that both ends quantify over all apportionments instead of picking one.

  recorded >= SUM of every applicable pool  -> TRUE
  recorded <  the LARGEST single pool       -> FALSE
  between the two                           -> NULL, and genuinely so

I wrote the version this replaces, which answered `null` for ANY multi-pool rule. That declined two answers it already had, and hank is correct that it did. The two ends are exact: if the recorded total clears the SUM, there is NO apportionment that fails; if it is under the LARGEST single pool, there is NO apportionment that succeeds. Attribution only matters in the middle band, and the middle band is where it still returns null. So this is strictly more answerable and no less honest -- which is the claim, and it holds.

AND THE DIRECTION OF THE CHANGE IS THE SAFE ONE, which is what I checked hardest, because the summation defect this module already carries a scar from went the other way: that defect compared ONE total against a SUM it then reported as a SINGLE TARGET and reported a PASS in the middle band. This change makes TRUE require clearing the SUM -- the STRICTEST reading available -- so the band that used to pass wrongly is exactly the band that now returns null. A reversal that made TRUE easier would have been the old defect wearing a new justification; this makes it harder.

ATTACK (b) -- AN EMPTY APPLICABLE SET IS NEVER A PASS, and this is the part worth the most. The code records that the FIRST VERSION OF THIS VERY CHANGE SHIPPED THE ORIGINAL DEFECT THROUGH A DIFFERENT DOOR: for Ohio, Indiana and both Pennsylvania chapters every requirement identifies its audience in prose, so nothing matched, `applicable` was empty, the target summed to 0, and a caregiver with ZERO recorded hours came back `meets: true` -- with the `unmapped_requirements` caveat sitting on the same response as the boolean that contradicted it.

"An empty requirement set is indistinguishable from a satisfied one once it has been summed" is this module's own sentence about the WV vocabulary bug, and it recurred inside the fix for it. A boolean now requires a NON-EMPTY applicable set, and the reason distinguishes the two ways a set can be empty -- "we could not read who this applies to" is NOT "this person has no obligation", and only the rule's author can say which. That distinction is the whole value of the change and it is the one a simplifier would collapse.

It was found by DRIVING ALL SIX SEEDED RULES; the code says "a verdict-only arm would not have." That is the correct account of why it was findable.

ATTACK (c) -- A WINDOW THAT COULD NOT BE COMPUTED IS NOT ZERO HOURS. NO_HIRE_DATE returns a total of 0, and 0 against any requirement is FALSE -- which would report every staff member with no recorded hire date as NON-COMPLIANT. A confident wrong answer manufactured from a missing field, and the same shape as the empty-set pass one direction over. Handled, and named as the same class rather than as a separate bug, which is the thing that makes it unlikely to come back a third time.

The join is SERVER-SIDE behind `include_staff`, so a caller cannot hand the evaluator a roster of its own choosing and have the compliance verdict computed from it.
